text.p: "Spin doctors", "hired-gun" strategists and image consultants are standard fare on the U.S. campaign trail these days, but most Japanese politicians seem content to rely on anonymous advisers and old-style stumping.
Still, with a new electoral system that in theory favours issues and images over personal ties, plus a large chunk of uncommitted voters, some experts say change may be in store.
"In the United States, there are many consultants and strategists, but we don't have that kind of real strategist," said Yasunori Sone, a Keio University political scientist.
"But if Japanese political campaigns shift from local canvassing to more U.S.-style advertising, probably there will be a change (in advisers)," Sone said.

A Lower House election on October 20 will be the nation's first under a new system designed to encourage electioneering based on party politics and policy debate instead of personal loyalties and pork barrel.

The new system features 300 single-seat constituencies and 200 decided by proportional representation in 11 regional blocs instead of the old multi-member districts where candidates could win by appealing to narrow special interests.
New rules on campaigning also allow greater scope for TV ads, previously confined to brief, dull and identically formatted statements by wooden-faced candidates on state TV.

Japanese politicians have traditionally exhibited little of the image-awareness that helped create a whole business out of political consulting in the United States, largely because the key determinant of victory has been political machines rather than broad appeals to voters through impersonal media.

That has meant mobilising votes through candidates' support groups and local organisations while appealing to the uncommitted mostly through street-corner speeches and vans with loudspeakers blaring out a candidate's name and a slogan.
"Being close to your local 'ikebana' (flower arrangement) group is more important than looking good on television," said one former aide to a Japanese member of parliament.
Some sniffed a change in the 1993 polls when self-styled reformists, including rebels from the conservative Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), ended the LDP's 38-year grip on power.

"That election focused on an image war -- how to differentiate images among individual politicians and parties," said one former journalist who has tried his hand at political consulting. "But there was no accumulated know-how in Japan."
Morihiro Hosokawa, who took power in the 1993 elections as the head of an anti-LDP coalition, grabbed headlines for his rare efforts to cultivate a media-friendly image.

For help with its television ads this time, the LDP -- now back in power as the main partner in Japan's ruling coalition -- has turned to the giant Dentsu advertising group, which has highlighted Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's well-known skills as traditional "kendo" swordsman in a spot ad.
The main opposition Shinshinto is also relying on a Dentsu subsidiary, while other parties have turned to rival agencies.
But many candidates remain wary of media handlers and paid image consultants, preferring instead to rely on a trusted circle of behind-the-scenes advisers, political insiders say.

"Most politicians still look down on that kind of thing," said one Shinshinto staffer. "They reluctantly listen to advice about what they should wear on television, but there is no consultant business like in the United States."

Some analysts foresee a greater role for professional consultants, but others say there is likely to be little scope for American-style high-profile "hired guns" willing to impart advice to candidates of any political ilk for a price.
"Here in Japan it's still kind of tribal. Everyone is tied to some political group. Advisers tend to be shadow people, they don't put up their shingle," another political aide said.
How popular "attack ads," which U.S. candidates use to try to discredit rivals, might become also remains in doubt given a mostly "feel good" Japanese advertising culture, analysts said.

On Monday the Shinshinto made a formal complaint to prosecutors over what it called "illegal wording" in an LDP newspaper ad which taunted the opposition party over its election pledge to keep the sales tax at three percent for now.

"Which is the real Shinshinto?" asked the LDP ad, saying party leaders had in the past proposed rises to seven, 10 and 15 percent. Shinshinto Secretary-General Takeo Nishioka lashed back in a statement: "The LDP advertisement distorts the facts and leads citizens to misunderstand our party's platform."
